title: What the Old Man Does Is Always Right
text:
An old peasant couple owned little except a horse. One day the wife suggested that her husband take the horse to the market in town and exchange it for something more useful. "Whatever you do will be right," she said.

On the road he met a man with a cow and traded the horse for it. Then he traded the cow for a sheep, the sheep for a fat goose, the goose for a hen, and finally the hen for a sack of rotten apples.

At the inn, two rich Englishmen heard his story and laughed. His wife would surely give him a beating, they said. The old man said she would give him a kiss. They bet him a bushel of gold coins against his sack of apples and went home with him to see.

As he told her each trade, the wife was delighted. A cow meant milk, butter and cheese. A sheep was even better: wool and sheep's milk. A goose meant a goose to roast. A hen would lay eggs and hatch chickens. And the rotten apples? Only that morning a neighbor's wife had refused to lend her even one rotten apple; now she could lend her a whole sack. She gave her husband a kiss.

The Englishmen paid the bushel of gold without complaint. A wife who believed her husband always did right, they said, was worth the money.
lesson: Meeting a partner's mistakes with good humor rather than blame can be worth more than any trade. A household rich in trust has wealth of its own.
people: An old peasant, his wife, two Englishmen
source: Hans Christian Andersen, What the Old Man Does Is Always Right (Hvad Fatter gjor, det er altid det Rigtige), 1861
